extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and general readers interested in psychological theories of humor (humor researchers, psychology students, writers studying humor)
extracted.subtask_description: Use Benign Violation Theory as a framework to analyze, predict, or produce humor: identify whether a situation is a violation, whether it is perceived as benign, and whether those perceptions occur simultaneously. The page explains what counts as violations, how benignness can be established, and why humor can fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Violation
rubrics_metrics.description: A situation that threatens one’s beliefs about how the world should be — something that seems threatening, unsettling, or wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes threats to physical well-being (e.g., tickling, play fighting), psychological well-being (insults, sarcasm), and behaviors that break norms: social (strange behaviors, flatulence), cultural (unusual accents, Borat scenes), linguistic (puns, malapropisms), logic (absurdities, non-sequiturs), and moral (disrespectful behavior, bestiality). A Violation is necessary for humor but by itself is usually not sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benignness
rubrics_metrics.description: The violation must be perceived as benign — it needs to seem okay, safe, or acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the violation does not also seem benign, it will not produce humor. The page highlights three specific mechanisms by which a violation can be perceived as benign (see separate entries): alternative norms, commitment to a violated norm, and psychological distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneity of perceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Both perceptions — that the situation is a violation and that it is benign — must occur simultaneously for humor to arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor requires that observers hold both the sense of threat/unexpectedness and the sense of harmlessness at the same time (e.g., play fighting is physically threatening but simultaneously harmless). If these perceptions do not co-occur, laughter does not follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative norms (one way a violation can seem benign)
rubrics_metrics.description: A violation can seem benign when there are alternative norms or alternative interpretations that make one interpretation acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in a pun, one meaning of a phrase may be nonsensical (violation) while the alternate meaning makes sense (benign). This alternative-norm framing can render a violation humorous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commitment to the violated norm (audience differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: A violation may be perceived as more or less benign depending on the audience’s commitment to the norm being violated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: men may find sexist jokes funnier than women do because of differing commitment to the violated norm. Differences in personal or group commitment to norms change whether a violation reads as benign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological distance (temporal/spatial/social distance as benigning factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Greater psychological distance can make a violation seem more benign and therefore more humorous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captures ideas like “comedy is tragedy plus time”: if an event is temporally, socially, or spatially distant from the audience, its threatening aspects may be reduced and the violation perceived as benign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimal violation intensity (balance: not too tame, not too malign)
rubrics_metrics.description: The strength or intensity of the violation must be balanced: if it is too tame (strictly benign) or too aggressive/malign, it will not be funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: play fighting ceases to elicit laughter when the attack stops (too benign) or becomes too aggressive (malign). Jokes similarly fail when they are either too tame or too risqué; there is a sweet spot in perceived severity for humor to occur.
